lesson.title: What is a sensor?
lesson.subtitle: Turning heat, light and water into numbers

video.title: What is a sensor?
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph Mwangi — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: School gate at dusk, orange sky. Joseph locks the computer room door. A solar lamp on a pole beside the gate glows on by itself. A pupil with a school bag points up at it, puzzled; Joseph looks up too, then at the camera.
scenes.animation: Sky darkens over 2 s; the lamp glows on with a soft pop. Quick push-in on the pupil’s pointing hand.
scenes.narration: Every evening, this lamp switches on by itself. Today a pupil asked me, “Sir, who switched it on?” Nobody touched it. So who — or what — noticed it was getting dark?
scenes.sound: Evening crickets; soft chime as the lamp lights; music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Character: illustrated computer studies teacher, ink outlines. A generic solar lamp with a small panel on top; no brand names.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the IoT track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: what a sensor is — and how devices turn the world around us into numbers.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: Split screen. Left: a pupil’s face with small icons beside the eyes, ears and hand. Right: the solar lamp, with a small sensor on top ringed in teal; a teal wave travels from the sensor down to the bulb, which lights up.
scenes.animation: Sense icons pop 200 ms apart; the teal wave travels down in 1 s, then the bulb glows.
scenes.narration: Your eyes, ears and skin notice the world around you. Devices can notice things too. Many solar lamps have a light sensor. When it notices the daylight fading, it sends a signal, and the lamp switches on.
scenes.sound: Soft tick for each icon; gentle hum as the bulb lights.
scenes.vids: Keep the face simple and friendly. Show the signal as a moving teal line, not text.

scenes.visual: Five round cards pop up in a row: a sun with heat lines, a light bulb, a water drop, a running figure, a sound wave. Under each, a thin teal line wiggles like a signal and ends in a small blank number box.
scenes.animation: Cards pop 250 ms apart; each signal line wiggles, then settles into its box.
scenes.narration: Sensors can notice heat, light, moisture, movement and sound. Each one turns what it notices into a number, or a signal — a message carried by a change, like a small electric current that rises and falls.
scenes.sound: A soft tick for each card.
scenes.vids: Hold all five cards together for 3 seconds at the end so viewers can take them in.

scenes.visual: Clean card on white with the IoT track chip. A thermometer icon on the left, an arrow, then a number box on the right.
scenes.animation: Arrow draws left to right in 600 ms; the number box pops.
scenes.narration: So: a sensor notices something in the world and turns it into a number or signal. The number it gives at one moment is called a reading.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A classroom. A teacher rests the back of her hand on a pupil’s forehead; a thought bubble shows a small warm sun. Then a thermometer appears beside the pupil, and the sun in the bubble turns into a number box.
scenes.animation: Thought bubble pops; the sun morphs into the number box in 400 ms.
scenes.narration: Your hand is a natural sensor. Touch a pupil’s forehead and it says “warm”. But “warm” is hard to write down or compare. A thermometer senses the same heat and gives a number — 37.8 degrees — that anyone can read.
scenes.vids: Illustrated classroom; the pupil looks calm and smiling, not ill. No medical setting.

scenes.visual: Amina Bello pops in at her classroom, gesturing to three objects on a desk: a loudspeaker, a wall thermometer and an open notebook with lines of readings. Three answer cards drop in, one picture each.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check from my classroom! I have a loudspeaker, a thermometer and a notebook of weather readings. Which one is the sensor?
scenes.sound: Three gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The thermometer card gets a blue check badge. The notebook card shows a small box icon (it only stores); the loudspeaker card shows sound waves going out, not in.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: The thermometer. It senses heat and turns it into a number. The notebook stores readings, but senses nothing. The loudspeaker makes sound instead of sensing it.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: Fast montage of three panels: a thermometer on a classroom wall; a probe pushed into a school garden bed beside seedlings; a phone whose microphone, camera lens and a tilt arrow are ringed in teal as it turns sideways.
scenes.animation: Each panel slides in from the right, about 5 seconds each. Keep motion simple and readable on a small screen.
scenes.narration: Sensors are everywhere. A thermometer on the classroom wall. A probe in the school garden that reads how wet the soil is. And in a phone: a microphone for sound, a camera for light, and a movement sensor that notices when you turn it.
scenes.vids: Use flat icons from the Darsi set. Show a generic phone with no logos or app screens.

scenes.visual: Four columns appear: a probe in soil (sense); a small screen showing one bar (show); a teacher’s head with a thought bubble beside a small chip (decide); a pump spraying seedlings and a buzzer with sound lines (act).
scenes.animation: Columns appear 300 ms apart; a teal arrow runs left to right through all of them.
scenes.narration: A sensor only measures. A display shows the reading — a screen, a dial, a thermometer’s scale. An actuator acts — a pump that waters, a motor that turns a fan, a buzzer that sounds. In between, a person or a small computer decides.
scenes.sound: Soft click as each column appears.
scenes.vids: Keep all four columns on screen for at least 4 seconds. Generic shapes, no product designs.

scenes.visual: Joseph stands by the school garden. A probe sits in a dry bed; a small pump with a hose waits beside it. Two answer cards bounce in: a probe and a pump.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. In an automatic watering system, a probe finds the soil is dry, and a pump switches on. Which part is the actuator?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight ‘pump’.

scenes.visual: The pump card gets the check badge and sprays water. Then three summary cards line up: a thermometer (sense), a small screen (show), a cog (act).
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: The pump — it acts. The probe is the sensor. So remember: sensors notice the world and turn it into numbers. Displays show them. Actuators act.
scenes.vids: Hold the three cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Joseph’s classroom. Three bowls on a desk: blue-tinted, plain, orange-tinted. A pupil has one hand in the blue bowl and one in the orange; classmates watch. Then both hands go into the middle bowl and the pupil laughs, puzzled. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Units and scales’.
scenes.animation: Hands dip, then move to the middle bowl. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: three bowls of water — cold, room temperature and warm. Pupils put one hand in the cold, one in the warm, then both in the middle. Their hands disagree! That’s why we use sensors that give numbers.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: A loudspeaker, a wall thermometer and a notebook of weather readings: which one is the sensor?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the thermometer senses heat and turns it into a number on its scale.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the notebook only stores readings, and the loudspeaker makes sound. The thermometer senses heat.

checkpoints.prompt: A probe finds the soil is dry, and a pump switches on. Which part is the actuator?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the pump acts on the world: it moves water. The probe is the sensor.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — the probe senses that the soil is dry. The pump is the actuator: it does the watering.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3-minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “What is a sensor?”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and a teal (#14b8a6) track accent; no gradients or blur. Main character: Mr Joseph Mwangi, a computer studies teacher. Follow the script scene by scene: a solar lamp at a school gate switches on at dusk; devices that notice heat, light, moisture, movement and sound; the definition of a sensor; the hand-on-forehead analogy; a quiz pause; sensors in a thermometer, a garden probe and a phone; sense, show, decide, act; a second quiz pause; recap; end with the three-bowls classroom test. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos or brand names on screen.
